title: Davenant: just from inherent; justified from imputed
source_text: XXIV. Monet istud Davenantius Episcopus Sarisburiensis, qui de doctrina Justificationis Reformatorum omnium accuratissime scripsit, & maximo cum Scholae Orthodoxae applausu. Nam libro de Justitia habituali, cap. 27. Illud, inquit, obiter observetis velim, nos haud affirmare denominationem justi in Scriptura sumi a forma extrinseca, sed justificati. Justi enim quemadmodum & sancti in Scripturis vocantur nonnulli ab inchoata justitia in ipsis inhaerente: sed justificati dicuntur a perfectissima Christi justitia ipsis imputata. Et ejusdem libri capite tertio duas hasce propositiones sigillatim probat & explicat, Primo, Donari sive infundi omnibus justificatis habitualem quandam, sive inhaerentem justitiam. Deinde, In hac infusa, sive inhaerente justitia fideles & renovatos omnes vocari & censeri justos, idque ab ipso Deo.
pass_a_gloss: Davenant, bishop of Salisbury, who wrote most accurately of all on the Reformers’ doctrine of Justification and with the greatest applause of the Orthodox school, warns of this. For in his book on Habitual Justice, chapter 27, he says: I would have you observe in passing that we by no means affirm that the denomination of the just in Scripture is taken from an extrinsic form, but that of the justified. For some are called just in the Scriptures, as also holy, from inchoate righteousness inhering in them; but they are called justified from the most perfect righteousness of Christ imputed to them. And in the third chapter of the same book he proves and explains two propositions one by one: First, that a certain habitual or inherent righteousness is given or infused to all the justified. Then, that in this infused or inherent righteousness all the faithful and renewed are called and reckoned just, and that by God himself.
pass_b_english: Davenant: “just” from inherent inchoate form; “justified” from Christ’s perfect imputed righteousness.
All justified receive infused habitual justice by which God also calls them just.
